items.title: Bias in Data Collection and Analysis

source_refs.note: 'Bias in Data Collection and Analysis' under topic 7.6, as printed (PDF 101-102, printed 97-98).

blocks.text: Bias in data collection occurs when data does not fairly represent all groups. This can happen due to limited data sources or unfair sampling methods. Biased data leads to inaccurate and misleading analysis results. During analysis, personal assumptions may also introduce bias. Such bias can affect decision-making and reinforce unfair outcomes. Identifying and mitigating bias is essential for reliable results. Therefore, careful data collection and objective analysis are necessary to ensure fairness. Here are simple examples of bias in data collection and analysis:

items: Survey Bias: A survey about student performance is conducted only in top-performing schools, ignoring average or low-performing schools.
Sampling Bias: A health study includes only young adults, so results do not represent older people.
Gender Bias: A hiring dataset contains mostly male candidates, leading the model to favour male applicants.
Geographical Bias: Data collected only from urban areas is used to make decisions for rural populations.
Confirmation Bias: A researcher focuses only on data that supports their belief and ignores contradictory results.
